name: LTC1624CS8#TRPBF
title: LTC1624: SO-8 current mode controller for an external N-channel MOSFET
summary: A fixed 200 kHz, current mode switching regulator controller in an 8-lead SO that drives one external N-channel MOSFET through a bootstrapped floating driver. It builds step-down, boost, SEPIC and positive-to-negative converters from 3.5 V to 36 V inputs, with a 1.19 V ±1% reference, 95% maximum duty cycle and an external sense resistor that sets the current limit. Burst Mode operation keeps light-load efficiency high, and the ITH/RUN pin carries compensation, soft start and a micropower shutdown (16 µA typical).
key_figures: TG rise and fall 50ns typ into 3000pF

pins.name: SENSE-
pins.function: Negative input of the current comparator, taken to the far end of RSENSE from VIN. The fixed offsets between this pin and VIN, divided by RSENSE, set the current thresholds. Keep it within 15 V below VIN and no more than 0.3 V below ground.

pins.name: ITH/RUN
pins.function: Error amplifier output, where the loop compensation network connects, and the run control. A higher voltage raises the current comparator's trip point; the working range is 1.19 V to 2.4 V. Below 0.8 V the part shuts down, every function stops and TG is held low.

pins.name: VFB
pins.function: Feedback input, fed from a resistor divider on the output; regulates to 1.19 V.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground. Return it to the negative terminals of COUT and CIN and to the Schottky diode's anode.

pins.name: SW
pins.function: Switch node, to the inductor. In a step-down converter it swings from one Schottky drop below ground up to VIN.

pins.name: TG
pins.function: Gate drive for the external N-channel MOSFET, from a floating driver whose swing is INTVCC riding on the SW voltage.

pins.name: BOOST
pins.function: Supply of the floating topside driver; the bootstrap capacitor CB returns to this pin. In step-down use it swings from INTVCC to VIN + INTVCC; in other topologies, with SW at 0 V, it sits at INTVCC.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Main supply and positive input of the current comparator. Decouple it to ground close to the pin.

circuits.title: Figure 1. High Efficiency Step-Down Converter
circuits.description: A 4.8 V to 28 V input is stepped down to 3.3 V at 2 A. The 0.05 Ω sense resistor in the drain of the Si4412DY sets the peak current; the switch node feeds a 10 µH inductor with an MBRS340T3 catch diode. 35.7k over 20k sets the output from the 1.19 V reference, 470 pF and 6.8k compensate the loop at ITH/RUN, and 1000 pF filters the sense input. CB, 0.1 µF from BOOST to SW, supplies the floating gate drive.

circuits.title: Figure 2. Setting the LTC1624 Output Voltage
circuits.description: The feedback divider is taken from the output node after the inductor: R2 from VOUT to VFB, R1 from VFB to the chip's ground, with 100 pF across R1 at the pins. Because the divider taps the output itself, it can sense the voltage at a remote load.
notes: VOUT = 1.19V × (1 + R2/R1). With remote sensing, a local 100 Ω from L1 to R2 keeps the output from running high if the sense lead opens.

circuits.title: Figure 3(a). ITH/RUN Pin Interfacing: logic gate through a diode
circuits.description: An inverting logic gate on a 3.3 V or 5 V supply pulls ITH/RUN low through D1 to shut the converter down; with the gate output high the diode is off and CC, RC compensate as usual.

circuits.title: Figure 3(b). ITH/RUN Pin Interfacing: open-drain N-channel MOSFET
circuits.description: A small N-channel MOSFET from ITH/RUN to ground shuts the converter down when its gate is driven high.

circuits.title: Figure 3(c). ITH/RUN Pin Interfacing: soft start
circuits.description: Soft start: R1 charges C1 from a supply, and D1 (anode at ITH/RUN, cathode at C1) lets the ITH/RUN voltage climb only as C1 charges, so the internal current limit ramps up with it. An N-channel MOSFET is connected across C1.

circuits.title: Figure 4. Plugging into the Cigarette Lighter
circuits.description: Input protection for a car's 12 V line: a series diode rated for 50 A peak blocks reverse battery, and a 1.5KA24A transient suppressor from VIN to ground clamps load dump.
notes: The suppressor must stay off at double-battery (24 V) and still clamp below the converter's breakdown.

circuits.title: Figure 5. Modifying Burst Mode Operation
circuits.description: A step-down converter with Q1 (2N2222) added: its base on VOUT and emitter resistor R* to ground make it a current source of about 180 µA, which pulls through a 100 Ω resistor in series with SENSE– and puts 18 mV across it. That offset cancels the burst comparator's own offset, so the top MOSFET is driven every cycle and the converter keeps a constant frequency down to IOUT(MIN).
notes: The LTC1624's ITH/RUN, VFB, BOOST and GND connections are those of a step-down converter such as Figure 1.

circuits.title: Figure 6. Boost Converter
circuits.description: The basic step-up arrangement. RSENSE sits between VIN and the inductor, with SENSE– at the inductor end; the MOSFET's source and the SW pin go to ground, the drain node feeds the output through D1, and R2 over R1 set the output.

circuits.title: Figure 7. SEPIC Converter
circuits.description: The basic SEPIC: L1 and the grounded-source MOSFET form the boost half, the coupling capacitor C1 carries the drain swing to L2 and D1, and the output may be above or below the input. L1 and L2 may share one core.

circuits.title: Figure 8. Positive-to-Negative Converter

The chip's GND pin is tied to –VOUT so that the feedback is positive with respect to it; R1 from system ground to VFB and R2 from VFB to –VOUT set the output, and D1 returns the inductor current from –VOUT to the switch node.

operation.text: Fixed 200 kHz, peak current mode. The oscillator sets an RS latch each cycle to turn the external MOSFET on, and current comparator I1 resets it when the inductor current reaches a level set by the ITH/RUN voltage, driven by error amplifier EA. EA compares VFB with the 1.19 V reference; more load pulls VFB down slightly, ITH/RUN rises, and the average inductor current follows the load. While the top MOSFET is off an internal bottom MOSFET turns on for roughly 300 ns to 400 ns to recharge the bootstrap capacitor CB.
Duty cycle can reach 95%. A dropout detector counts how many cycles the MOSFET stays on and now and then forces a short off time so CB can recharge.

Pulling ITH/RUN below 0.8 V shuts the part down with IQ under 30 µA; logic can drive the pin directly (Figure 3a, 3b). Released, an internal 2.5 µA source charges CC; at 0.8 V the loop starts and EA pulls ITH/RUN up toward 2.4 V while the output is low. In normal running ITH/RUN moves between 1.19 V and 2.4 V with load. Ramping ITH/RUN slowly from 1.19 V to 2.4 V (Figure 3c) ramps the peak current limit in proportion, from about 10mV/RSENSE at 1.4 V to 160mV/RSENSE at 2.4 V, which limits inrush and can sequence supplies.
Comparator OV turns the top MOSFET off and holds it off while the output overshoots by more than 7.5% (VFB above the 1.28 V lockout).

At light load the MOSFET switches in bursts. When comparator B sees ITH/RUN below 1.5 V and the RSENSE voltage stays under comparator I2's offset (about 20 mV) for a full cycle, the top and internal bottom drives stop on the following cycles until ITH/RUN climbs back over 1.5 V. Burst Mode begins at roughly 8mV/RSENSE, about 8% of maximum output current. Smaller inductors make it start at higher load and lower the burst frequency. Figure 5 adds an 18 mV offset in series with SENSE– to keep constant-frequency operation to lower currents; cycle skipping still starts near 1% of maximum current, set by the 450 ns minimum on-time.

An internal regulator makes the 5 V INTVCC that powers the drivers and internal circuits. An internal high voltage diode DB charges CB from INTVCC each off cycle while SW is low, and a small internal N-channel MOSFET pulls SW to ground after each on time to keep CB fully charged. When TG turns on, CB's voltage is placed across the MOSFET gate and source, SW rises to VIN and BOOST to VIN + INTVCC. CB should be at least 50 times the MOSFET's input capacitance; 0.1 µF usually suffices.

Feeding BOOST from the output saves input current because the driver current is then scaled by (duty cycle)/(efficiency): for 5 V outputs a small Schottky such as a CMDSH-3 from VOUT to BOOST (Figure 10); for 3.3 V and lower outputs extra circuitry is needed. In a 20 V to 5 V converter, 5 mA of INTVCC current becomes about 1.5 mA at the input. For VIN below 7 V a Schottky from VIN to BOOST raises the gate drive. BOOST to SW must stay at or below 7.8 V.

The gate swing is INTVCC, typically 5 V, so logic level MOSFETs are needed; below 5 V input, sublogic level parts. In boost, SEPIC and inverting circuits gate drive is about 5 V for VIN above 5.6 V and VIN – 0.6 V below 5 V. Check BVDSS: many logic level MOSFETs stop at 30 V. Choose by RDS(ON), CRSS, input voltage and current. Below about 20 V a larger MOSFET improves efficiency at high current; above about 20 V transition losses dominate and a part with higher RDS(ON) and lower CRSS does better. For a boost converter that 20 V boundary applies to VOUT, and for SEPIC and inverting converters to VIN + VOUT.

At the fixed 200 kHz small inductances are favoured; for step-down circuits 5 µH to 68 µH is typical, for boost, SEPIC and inverting circuits 10 µH to 100 µH. Larger inductance lowers ripple and core loss but needs more turns and copper. Ferrite has very low core loss but saturates abruptly, so the peak current must stay below saturation; molypermalloy and Kool Mµ toroids are low-loss alternatives. The inductor's saturation current must exceed the maximum set by RSENSE.

The step-down Schottky conducts in the off time and is most stressed in a short circuit (VOUT = 0 V), carrying ISC(PK) at nearly 100% duty. In a boost converter the diode sees VOUT in reverse and carries the output current; in SEPIC and inverting converters it sees VOUT + VIN. Boost converters have no short-circuit protection: the inductor current is then limited only by the source. MBR130LT3 is a suggested Schottky for boost and SEPIC circuits.

The step-down input current is a square wave of duty about VOUT/VIN, so CIN must be a low ESR part rated for the RMS current; ripple ratings are often for 2000 hours, so derate or choose a higher temperature part. COUT is chosen by ESR. Tantalums must be surge tested, since a battery connected suddenly can destroy untested ones. A boost converter's input capacitor is less critical, typically 10 µF to 100 µF with ESR around 0.3 Ω; its output capacitor carries large RMS ripple. Inverting converters have high ripple current in both capacitors.

The minimum recommended on-time is 450 ns. Below 9% duty cycle the part may skip cycles: ripple current rises but regulation holds. For a step-down converter this restricts input voltage only for VOUT below 2.2 V with 30 V MOSFETs. In a boost converter the minimum on-time limits how close VIN may come to VOUT before the output overshoots and trips the overvoltage comparator. SEPIC and inverting designs are affected only below about 2.5 V output.

Four losses dominate: the LTC1624's VIN current (IQ plus gate drive current), I²R losses in the MOSFET, RSENSE and inductor, topside MOSFET transition losses (significant at about 20 V input and above), and the Schottky drop. Example: at 50% duty with RDS(ON) = 0.05 Ω, RL = 0.15 Ω and RSENSE = 0.05 Ω the effective resistance is 0.2 Ω, costing 2% to 8% at VOUT = 5 V from 0.5 A to 2 A; a 0.5 V diode at 50% duty costs about 5%. Capacitor ESR and core losses usually add under 2%.

A load step first moves VOUT by ∆ILOAD • ESR, then the loop restores it over several cycles; watching for overshoot or ringing checks stability. The ITH components of Figure 1 compensate most designs. Switching in a load with large (>1 µF) bypass capacitance drops VOUT sharply; the remedy is to slow the load switch's rise time.

A car battery line can carry load dump (spikes to about 60 V lasting hundreds of milliseconds), reverse battery and double battery (24 V jump starts). Figure 4's series diode blocks reverse polarity and its transient suppressor clamps load dump. Though the part is rated to 36 V, most designs are limited to 30 V by the MOSFET BVDSS.

L1 and L2 see the same voltage throughout the cycle, so they may be wound on one core; with L1 = L2 on one core, use 2L for L in the equations. A Coiltronics CTX10-4 (10 µH, two windings) gives 10 µH at 4 A with the windings paralleled, or two 10 µH, 2 A inductors split, so L = 20 µH.

With GND on –VOUT, shutdown needs ITH/RUN pulled below 0.8 V relative to –VOUT; its normal range is –VOUT (shutdown) to –VOUT + 2.4 V (maximum output current). In Figure 15, M2, M3 and R3 shift TTL levels down: M3 drives M2's gate in shutdown and M2 pulls ITH/RUN to –VOUT.

Keep signal and power grounds apart, returning GND (pin 4) to COUT's negative plate. Run VFB (pin 3) straight to R1, R2, which connect between COUT's positive plate and signal ground, with the 100 pF capacitor close to the part. Join VIN to the input at the same point as RSENSE and run SENSE– and VIN side by side at minimum spacing, with their filter capacitor close to the part. Put CIN's positive plate as close to RSENSE as possible and CIN close to the VIN and GND pins, since it supplies the MOSFET's AC current and recharges the bootstrap capacitor. Keep SW away from small-signal nodes and join M1, L1 and D1 tightly at the switch node.
